'''''Jatropha podagrica''''' is a [[species]] of [[Flowering plant|flowering]], [[Caudex|caudiciform]] [[Succulent plant|succulent]] plant in the spurge family, [[Euphorbiaceae]], aligning it closely with related genera such as [[Croton (plant)|''Croton'']], ''[[Euphorbia]]'' and ''[[Ricinus]]'' (castor bean), among others.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-104848|title=Jatropha podagrica Hook. — The Plant List|website=www.theplantlist.org|access-date=2020-01-13}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/12800226|title=Tropicos {{!}} Name - !Jatropha podagrica Hook.|website=www.tropicos.org|access-date=2020-01-13}}</ref> It is native to the [[Neotropical realm|neotropics]] of [[Central America]] and southern [[Mexico]], but is grown as an [[Ornamental plant|ornamental]] plant in many parts of the world due to its unusual appearance and mature [[caudex]] development. Common names for the species include '''gout-plant''', '''gout-stalk''', '''Guatemalan rhubarb''', '''coral-plant''', '''Buddha-belly plant''', '''purging-nut''', '''physic-nut''', '''goutystalk nettlespurge''', '''Australian bottleplant''' (a geographical [[misnomer]]) and '''tartogo'''.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=http://www.llifle.com/Encyclopedia/SUCCULENTS/Family/Euphorbiaceae/22500/Jatropha_podagrica|title=Jatropha podagrica|website=www.llifle.com|access-date=2020-01-13}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.jaycjayc.com/jatropha-podagrica-buddha-belly/|title=Gouty stem of Jatropha podagrica (Buddha Belly Plant) {{!}} John&Jacq~s Garden|access-date=2020-01-13}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=http://www.stuartxchange.org/BuddhaBellyPlant|title=Buddha belly plant, Jatropha podagrica, Gout plant, Fo du shu : Philippine Medicinal Herbs / Alternative Medicine|website=www.stuartxchange.org|access-date=2020-01-13}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.flowersofindia.net/catalog/slides/Australian%20Bottle%20Plant.html|title=Jatropha podagrica - Australian Bottle Plant|website=www.flowersofindia.net|access-date=2020-01-13}}</ref>

==Description==
''J. podagrica'' is a [[caudiciform]] [[perennial]] [[herb]] growing up to 1 metre (3 feet) tall.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> The grey-green, knobby, swollen [[caudex]] has a bottle-like appearance, giving rise to some of the common names. Leaves are held on long fleshy yet stout [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] which emerge from the tip of the stem and radiate in all directions. Leaves are [[Glossary of leaf morphology|peltate]] and 3 or 5 lobed. Dense clusters of small, orange-red, flowers are held above the leaves on long slim [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]]. The clusters carry both male and female flowers and flowering continues for most of the year.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://www.childrens.health.qld.gov.au/poisonous-plant-guatemala-rhubarb-jatropha-podagrica/|title=Guatemala rhubarb (Jatropha podagrica) {{!}} Children's Health Queensland|last=Queensl|first=Children's Health|date=2017-07-18|website=Children’s Health Queensland|language=en-AU|access-date=2020-01-13}}</ref> Fruit are green capsules at first, becoming blackish-brown at maturity when they burst and scatter the seeds up to 4 metres (13 feet) away.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

When cut, the plant exudes a copious sticky sap which may cause [[dermatitis]] on contact.<ref name=":3" />

==Cultivation==
The swollen caudex, showy leaves, and colourful flowers make ''J. podagrica'' an attractive ornamental, and it is grown as an indoor plant in many parts of the world.

==Uses==
There are many traditional uses of ''J. podagrica'' in [[Traditional medicine|folk medicine]], with a number of significant research initiatives being undertaken into the species' potential health benefits. Industrial and practical uses include the plant's potential as a form of [[biofuel]], [[dye]], [[pest control]], plant [[Fertilizer|fertiliser]], [[soap]], and as a natural form of lighting or [[Kerosene lamp|lamp oil]] (typically [[kerosene]]), as well as for [[leather]] and [[Tanning (leather)|tanning]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

==Toxicity==
All parts of the plant are considered [[Toxicity|toxic]], in particular the seeds. The main toxins are a purgative oil and a phytotoxin or toxalbumin (curcin) similar to [[ricin]] in [[Ricinus|Ricinis]].<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.inchem.org/documents/pims/plant/jpoc.htm|title=Jatropha podagrica (PIM 647)|website=www.inchem.org|access-date=2020-01-13}}</ref>
